Authentication vs authorization: The first answers *who are you?* The second answers *what may you do?*
OAuth vs OIDC vs SAML: The first grants an app access to your stuff; the second adds "who the user is" on top of the first; the third is the older XML-based way to log in once for many apps.
Cookie vs localStorage vs sessionStorage: The first is sent to the backend with every request; the second keeps data in the browser indefinitely; the third is wiped when the tab closes.
Session vs JWT: The first: the backend keeps the login record and the browser holds only an ID. The second: the browser holds the whole signed record and the backend keeps nothing.
Encoding vs encryption vs hashing: The first changes format and anyone can reverse it (Base64); the second needs a key to reverse; the third is one-way and can't be reversed.
401 vs 403: The first: "I don't know who you are, log in." The second: "I know who you are, and the answer is no."
PUT vs PATCH: The first replaces the whole resource; the second changes only the fields you send.
Library vs framework: You call the first; the second calls your code.
Compiler vs interpreter: The first translates the whole program before running it; the second translates as it runs.
Git vs GitHub: The first is the version-control tool on your machine; the second is a website that hosts its repos.
`var` vs `let` vs `const` (JavaScript): The first is old and function-scoped; the second can be reassigned; the third can't. Default to the third.
Process vs thread: The first is a running program with its own memory; the second is a worker inside it that shares that memory.
Concurrency vs parallelism: The first: juggling many tasks by switching between them. The second: doing many tasks at the exact same moment on multiple cores.
Stack vs heap: The first: fast, small, automatic memory for function calls. The second: bigger memory for data that lives longer.
Container vs virtual machine: The first shares the host's OS kernel and starts in seconds; the second runs a whole separate OS.
Continuous delivery vs continuous deploy: The first: every change is *ready* to ship with a button press. The second: every change ships automatically.
Merge vs rebase: The first keeps both histories and adds a join commit; the second replays your commits on top of the other branch for a straight line.
Callback: A function you hand to another function so it can run it later.
Higher-order function: A routine that takes other routines as arguments or returns them, like `map` or `filter`.
Object-oriented programming (OOP): Organize code as class instances that bundle data with the methods that act on it.
Functional programming: Build software from pure, side-effect-free routines and immutable data.
Hash map: Key-value lookup that finds a value almost instantly, like a Python `dict` or a plain JS object.
Stack: Last in, first out, like a pile of plates (undo history).
Tree: Items arranged as parents and children, like folders. The DOM is one.
Binary search tree: A branching node structure kept sorted so you find things by going left or right at each node.
Binary search: Find an item in a sorted list by halving the area you look in each step.
Sorting algorithms: Ways to arrange items in order (divide-and-merge, pivot partitioning). The language's built-in one is usually enough.
Two pointers / sliding window: Walk through a list with a pair of index markers to avoid nested loops.
File permissions (`chmod`): Who may read, write, or run something on disk: owner, group, everyone.
SSH keys: A public/private credential pair that logs you in to a remote machine without a password; the public half goes on that machine.
HTTPS: The web's request protocol wrapped in an encrypted tunnel, so nobody in between can read or change the traffic.
HTTP status codes: Three-digit reply numbers: 2xx ok, 3xx go elsewhere, 4xx the client's mistake, 5xx the backend's mistake.
Server-Sent Events: A one-way stream where the backend keeps pushing updates to the browser.
HTTP/2 & HTTP/3: Newer versions of the web's request protocol that carry many requests at once over one connection; the latest runs on QUIC (UDP).
Latency vs bandwidth: The first: how long one trip takes. The second: how much fits through at once.
OWASP Top 10: A well-known ranked list of the most common, dangerous web app weaknesses, published by an open security foundation.
CSRF (Cross-site request forgery): A malicious page tricks your logged-in browser into firing off an action you didn't intend.
Clickjacking: Hiding your real page under a fake one so users press buttons they can't see.
Password hashing (bcrypt, Argon2): Deliberately slow one-way scrambling with a salt, so stolen lists of login secrets are hard to crack.
Encryption (symmetric vs asymmetric): Scrambling data so only key holders can read it. One kind uses a single shared key; the other uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock.
Zero trust: Never assume a request is safe just because it comes from "inside" the network; verify every time.
CVE: A public tracking number assigned to a known vulnerability, such as the one for Log4Shell.
Supply chain attack: Compromising you through a library or tool you depend on.
Session: The backend remembers you're logged in, usually via a cookie holding an ID.
SSO (Single Sign-On): Log in once, get into many apps (e.g. "Continue with Google" at work).
IdP (Identity Provider): The service that actually verifies who you are on behalf of other apps (Google, Okta, Entra).
Access token / refresh token: A short-lived pass for API calls, plus a longer-lived pass used to obtain new short-lived ones.
Passkeys / WebAuthn: Login without any secret phrase, using your device's fingerprint, face, or PIN. Resistant to phishing.
API key: A long secret string identifying which app is calling a service's interface.
Props & state: The first: inputs a component receives. The second: data a component remembers and changes.
Virtual DOM: A lightweight in-memory copy of the page's element tree that frameworks compare to find the minimum real changes.
SPA (Single-page app): One initial load; JavaScript swaps content as you navigate.
MPA (Multi-page app): Classic sites where each link loads a fresh document from the backend.
SSR (Server-side rendering): The backend builds the full HTML for each request. Faster first view, better SEO.
Islands architecture: Mostly static HTML with small, isolated interactive pockets of JavaScript.
Server components: UI pieces that run only on the backend and send finished markup, with no JS shipped to the browser for them.
Design tokens: Named values (colors, spacing, fonts) shared across a whole UI style system.
Native vs cross-platform vs hybrid: The first: separate code per OS (Swift, Kotlin) for the best performance; the second: one codebase compiled to both (Flutter, React's mobile toolkit); the third: a website wrapped in a thin OS-level shell.
App store review: A human plus automated check of your mobile build before it goes live in the marketplace; can take hours to days, and can reject you.
Push notifications: Messages delivered straight to a user's device even when your app isn't open, via Apple's or Google's delivery service.
Deep links / universal links: A URL that opens a specific screen inside your app, instead of a website.
Offline-first: Design the app to read and write on-device data by default, syncing with the backend whenever a connection shows up.
App bundle / APK / IPA: The installable package you ship: Android's AAB or older installer archive, and iOS's own archive format.
WebView: A mini browser embedded inside a native app, used to show online pages in place.
Responsive vs adaptive (mobile): The first: one flexible layout that reflows to fit any screen; the second: several fixed layouts, swapped in per screen size.
Mobile app signing: Cryptographically stamping your package so the OS and marketplace can trust it wasn't tampered with.
Crash reporting: Automatic capture of failure details from users' devices, so you find bugs you'd never hit yourself.
React Native bridge / new architecture (: How Meta's mobile toolkit lets JavaScript talk to platform code: the old way batches messages as JSON; the modern design lets scripts invoke platform functions directly.
RPC / gRPC: Invoking a function on another machine as if it were local; Google's version is a fast binary flavor.
API versioning: Keeping old interface behavior working (`/v1`, `/v2`) while you change things.
Serverless: You upload functions; the cloud runs and scales them, and you never manage machines.
Edge functions: On-demand cloud code running in data centers close to users.
SQL vs NoSQL: The first: tables with fixed columns and relations. The second: flexible shapes like documents or key-value pairs.
Index: A sorted lookup structure so the DB finds rows without scanning everything, like the back pages of a book.
N+1 query problem: Fetching a list, then one extra DB request per item: 101 round trips where 1 would do.
Connection pool: A set of reusable open DB links, so each request skips the slow handshake.
Row Level Security (RLS): Rules inside the DB deciding which records each user may see or change.
Client-server: One side asks, the other answers. The basic shape of the web.
Event-driven architecture: Parts of the system react to announcements like "order placed" instead of invoking each other directly.
Event sourcing: Save every change as a log entry; current state comes from replaying them.
Twelve-Factor App: A set of 12 rules for building software that deploys and scales cleanly in the cloud.
System design: Planning how the pieces of a large platform fit together to meet scale and reliability needs.
Design a URL shortener: Hash or count up a compact code, keep code-to-link pairs in a fast key-value database, and redirect on lookup.
Design a rate limiter: Keep a rolling counter of requests per user or IP in a fast store like Redis, and reject once it crosses the cap.
Design a news feed: Fan out each post to every follower's timeline at post time (fast reads, costly for celebrities) or merge timelines at read time (cheap writes, slower reads).
Read-heavy vs write-heavy: When lookups dominate, lean on caching and replicas; when inserts and updates dominate, lean on sharding and async processing.
Database replication vs sharding choice: The first copies every record to extra machines to scale lookups and add durability; the second splits records across machines to scale inserts and capacity.
Idempotent APIs in payments: Attach a client-generated unique value to a charge request so retrying a timed-out call can't bill the card twice.
Design a notification system (fan-out): One event goes onto a queue that spreads to separate push, email, and SMS workers, so one slow channel can't block the others.
Load shedding / graceful degradation: Under heavy traffic, deliberately drop or simplify some requests so the whole platform doesn't fall over.
Distributed ID generation (Snowflake IDs: Mint unique, roughly time-ordered keys on many machines at once without a central counter.
Coupling & cohesion: The first (keep it low): parts don't depend on each other's insides. The second (keep it high): related code lives together.
Code smell: A surface sign in a program that something might be wrong underneath.
Infrastructure as Code (IaC): Servers, networks, and DBs defined in text files instead of clicked together in a console.
Feature flags: On/off switches in the app to release functionality without redeploying.
Virtual machines (AWS EC2, Google Comput: A rented box in the cloud you fully control, with its own OS, like leasing a bare desktop instead of buying one.
Object storage (AWS S3, Google Cloud Sto: Keep any file as a named item with its own URL; no folder tree, and it scales to any size.
Managed SQL database (AWS RDS, Google Cl: A regular relational DB where the provider handles patching, backups, and scaling.
Managed NoSQL database (AWS DynamoDB, Go: A flexible, schema-less store for records, built to spread across many machines automatically.
Serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Google: Upload just your handler; the provider runs it on demand and bills only for the time it runs.
Containers-as-a-service (AWS Fargate, Go: Launch a packaged app image without provisioning or looking after the machines underneath it.
Managed Kubernetes (AWS EKS, Google Kube: The provider operates the container orchestrator's control plane for you; you only look after what's deployed on top.
Secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Go: A locked safe for passwords and API credentials, so they never sit in your code or config files.
VPC (AWS VPC, Google VPC, Azure Virtual: Your own isolated, walled-off slice of the provider's infrastructure, where you control what can reach what.
Monitoring & logs (AWS CloudWatch, Googl: The provider's built-in dashboards for tracking metrics and reading event records from everything you deploy.
Regions & availability zones: The first is a geographic area (like `us-east-1`); the second are separate data centers inside it, so one outage doesn't take everything down.
Autoscaling (AWS Auto Scaling, Google Cl: Add or remove machines on its own as traffic rises and falls, so you're not paying for idle capacity.
Single point of failure: One component whose breakdown takes everything down.
Unit test: Checks one small piece (a function) in isolation.
Integration test: Checks several pieces working together (e.g. code plus a real DB).
Test pyramid: Many fast isolated checks, fewer checks of combined pieces, and only a few slow end-to-end ones.
Test coverage: Percent of code lines your automated checks execute. A high number doesn't mean the checks are good.
Flaky test: An automated check that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change.
Lazy loading: Only fetch images or code when they're about to be needed.
Memory leak: RAM that's never freed, so the app gets slower and eventually crashes.
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: The first assumes no conflict and checks at save time; the second grabs exclusive hold of the row up front.
Pull request (PR): Asking to merge your branch, where teammates look it over first.
Conventional commits: A standard message format like `feat: add login` that tools can parse.
Tool use / function calling: Letting a model invoke your code (search, database, APIs) to get things done.
Data minimization: Only collect the personal information you actually need.
Cookie consent: Asking users for permission before setting non-essential trackers in their browser.
Terminal vs shell: The first is the window you type into; the second (bash, zsh) is the program that reads and runs your commands.
